d: A set of activities that look for defects and evaluate the quality of software work products. It covers both dynamic testing (running the software) and static testing (examining work products without running them).
tip: Testing is wider than test execution: planning, analysis, design and reviews are all testing activities.

d: The reason for testing. Typical objectives are finding defects, checking coverage, reducing the risk of poor quality, verifying requirements, validating that the product meets stakeholder needs and building confidence.
tip: Fixing defects is NOT a test objective; that is debugging. Improving the process is quality assurance, not testing.

d: A human action that produces an incorrect result, for example a developer misreading a requirement. Also called a mistake.
tip: Chain to remember: error (person) → defect (in the work product) → failure (seen when the code runs).

d: An imperfection or flaw in a work product, such as code, a requirement or a test script, that does not meet its requirements. Also called a bug or fault.
tip: A defect exists in the work product whether or not anyone has found it, and not every defect causes a failure.

d: An event in which a component or system does not do what it should, observed when the software is executed. A failure is usually caused by a defect but can also come from environmental conditions such as radiation or hardware faults.
tip: Failures are only visible during dynamic testing; static testing finds defects directly.

d: The underlying reason a problem happened, for example time pressure or unclear requirements leading to an error. Removing the root cause prevents similar defects in the future.
tip: Root cause analysis looks at why the error happened, not just where the defect is.

d: The development activity of finding, analysing and removing the cause of a failure. It includes reproducing the failure, diagnosing the defect and fixing it.
tip: Testing shows that defects exist; debugging removes them. Confirmation testing then checks the fix.

d: The degree to which a work product satisfies stated and implied needs of its stakeholders.
tip: Testing can measure and report quality, but it cannot add quality by itself.

d: Process-oriented, preventive activities that aim to make sure the right processes are used so that quality is built in. Abbreviated QA.
tip: QA = process and prevention. Testing is a form of quality control, which is product-oriented and corrective.

d: Product-oriented, corrective activities that check a work product meets the required quality. Testing is a major form of quality control.
tip: If the question is about evaluating the product, think QC; if it is about improving the process, think QA.

d: Checking that a work product meets its specified requirements: are we building the product right?
tip: Exam traps often swap verification and validation. Requirements met = verification; user needs met = validation.

d: Checking that a work product meets the needs of users and other stakeholders in its intended environment: are we building the right product?
tip: Acceptance testing is mostly about validation.

d: The set of test activities: test planning, test monitoring and control, test analysis, test design, test implementation, test execution and test completion. The activities are tailored to the context and often overlap or repeat.
tip: There is no single universal test process; it depends on the context (SDLC, risks, domain, constraints).

d: Defining the test objectives and choosing an approach that meets them within the constraints of the context. The result is usually a test plan.
tip: Planning decides what, how and when to test; it is revisited as the project goes on.

d: Continuously checking test progress and comparing actual results against the test plan, using test metrics.
tip: Monitoring gathers information; control acts on it.

d: Taking actions, such as re-prioritising tests or changing the schedule, so that testing meets its objectives when monitoring shows a deviation from the plan.
tip: Examples of control: re-prioritise tests when a risk materialises, change the schedule when an environment is late.

d: Analysing the test basis to identify testable features and define test conditions. It answers the question: what to test?
tip: Analysis produces test conditions; design turns them into test cases. Defects in the test basis are often found here.

d: Turning test conditions into test cases and other testware, identifying coverage items and test data requirements. It answers the question: how to test?
tip: Test techniques are mainly used during test design.

d: Creating or acquiring the testware needed for execution, for example test procedures, test data, test suites and the test environment, and building the test execution schedule.
tip: Ask: is everything in place to run the tests? That is implementation.

d: Running the tests according to the execution schedule, comparing actual with expected results, logging the outcome and reporting anomalies.
tip: Analysing anomalies to find their likely cause is part of execution.

d: Activities at a project milestone such as a release: archiving testware, closing the environment, checking defect reports, collecting lessons learned and writing the test completion report.
tip: Change requests or backlog items are created for defects that are still open.

d: The body of knowledge used as the basis for test analysis and design, for example requirements, user stories, designs or code.
tip: If you can derive tests from it, it is part of the test basis.

d: A testable aspect of a component or system identified as a basis for testing, such as a function, transaction or quality characteristic.
tip: Test condition = what to test; test case = how to test it.

d: A set of preconditions, inputs, actions, expected results and postconditions, developed from test conditions.
tip: A test case without an expected result is incomplete.

d: A sequence of test cases in execution order, with any actions needed to set up the preconditions and wrap up afterwards.
tip: Test procedures are built during test implementation.

d: A set of test cases or test procedures grouped to be executed in a specific test run.
tip: Organising test procedures into suites happens during test implementation.

d: Data needed for test execution, such as input values and the data in databases or files that the test relies on.
tip: Test data requirements are identified in test design; the data is created in test implementation.

d: The work product being tested, for example a component, a system or a document.
tip: The test object differs by test level: a component for component testing, the whole system for system testing.

d: The consequence or outcome of executing a test, such as pass, fail or blocked.
tip: A failed result triggers analysis and possibly a defect report.

d: The work products produced during testing, such as test plans, test cases, scripts, test data and reports.
tip: Testware is archived or handed over at test completion for reuse.

d: The ability to link elements of the test basis to related testware, such as requirements to test conditions, test cases, results and defects.
tip: Traceability supports coverage evaluation, impact analysis of changes and audits.

d: The degree, expressed as a percentage, to which specified coverage items have been exercised by a test suite.
tip: 100% coverage does not mean the software is defect-free.

d: Separating responsibility for testing from development, ranging from the author testing their own work to testers from outside the organisation.
tip: Independent testers find different defects, but too much independence can cause isolation and a blame culture.

d: A way of working where everyone on the team, with any skill set, shares responsibility for quality and can perform any task.
tip: Testers work closely with business representatives and developers, not as a separate gate at the end.

d: The activities performed at each stage of software development and how they relate to each other. Abbreviated SDLC. Models include sequential (waterfall, V-model), iterative and incremental ones.
tip: Good practices for any SDLC: every development activity has a test activity, and testers get involved early.

d: Performing testing earlier in the SDLC, for example reviewing requirements, writing tests before code, running static analysis and using continuous integration.
tip: Shift left costs extra effort up front but saves effort later.

d: A test-first approach in which developers write a failing unit test, write code until it passes, then refactor. Abbreviated TDD.
tip: TDD = developer tests at code level. ATDD and BDD start from acceptance criteria and behaviour.

d: A test-first approach where acceptance tests are written from the acceptance criteria before the feature is developed, in collaboration with the team. Abbreviated ATDD.
tip: In ATDD, tests come from acceptance criteria and are written before implementation.

d: A test-first approach that expresses the desired behaviour in plain language, often in Given/When/Then form, so stakeholders can understand the tests. Abbreviated BDD.
tip: Given/When/Then format points to BDD.

d: An approach that brings development and operations together, with a delivery pipeline built on continuous integration and continuous delivery.
tip: Benefits include fast feedback and automated regression tests; risks include the effort to set up the pipeline and tooling.

d: A meeting, often at the end of an iteration or project, where the team discusses what went well, what did not and what to improve.
tip: Retrospectives drive process improvement, including improvements to testing.

d: A group of test activities organised and managed together, tied to a stage of development: component, component integration, system, system integration and acceptance testing.
tip: Each level has its own objectives, test basis, test object, typical defects and responsibilities.

d: Testing individual components in isolation. Also called unit testing. It is usually done by developers in their development environment.
tip: It often needs test harnesses or unit test frameworks.

d: Testing the interfaces and interactions between components or systems. CTFL splits it into component integration testing and system integration testing.
tip: The focus is on interactions, not on the functionality of each part.

d: Testing the interfaces and interactions between components, often following an integration strategy such as bottom-up, top-down or big-bang.
tip: Usually the developers' responsibility.

d: Testing the overall behaviour and capabilities of a whole system, both functional and non-functional, often by an independent test team.
tip: System testing uses a representative test environment and checks end-to-end tasks.

d: Testing the interfaces between the system under test and other systems or external services.
tip: It needs test environments close to the operational environment.

d: Testing that focuses on validation and on showing readiness for deployment. Forms include user acceptance testing, operational acceptance testing, contractual and regulatory acceptance testing, and alpha and beta testing.
tip: Finding defects is not the main goal of acceptance testing; confidence and readiness are.

d: A group of test activities aimed at specific quality characteristics: functional, non-functional, black-box and white-box testing.
tip: Any test type can be performed at any test level.

d: Testing that evaluates what the system should do: its functional completeness, correctness and appropriateness.
tip: Functional = what it does; non-functional = how well it does it.

d: Testing how well the system behaves, against quality characteristics such as performance efficiency, compatibility, usability, reliability, security, maintainability and portability.
tip: Non-functional testing can and should start early, not only at the end.

d: Testing based on the specification of the test object, without reference to its internal structure.
tip: Black-box = specification-based; white-box = structure-based.

d: Testing based on the internal structure of the system, such as code, architecture or workflows.
tip: White-box testing can find defects even when the specification is vague or outdated.

d: Re-testing to confirm that an original defect has been fixed, by re-running the tests that failed or adding new tests for the change.
tip: Confirmation = did the fix work? Regression = did the fix break anything else?

d: Testing to confirm that a change, including a fix, has not caused adverse effects elsewhere in the system.
tip: Regression suites run often and grow over time, so they are strong candidates for automation.

d: Testing changes to a system in operation, triggered by modifications, upgrades, migration to another platform or the retirement of the system.
tip: The scope depends on the risk of the change, the size of the system and the size of the change.

d: Evaluating a change to decide its intended consequences, possible side effects and which areas of the system need regression testing.
tip: Impact analysis is harder when traceability is missing or documentation is out of date.

d: Testing that examines work products without executing them, through manual reviews or tool-based static analysis.
tip: Static testing finds defects directly and can be applied to non-executable work products such as requirements.

d: Testing that involves executing the software.
tip: Dynamic testing finds failures; static testing finds defects. They complement each other.

d: Tool-supported evaluation of code or other work products without running them, for example checking coding standards, complexity or data flow.
tip: Static analysis can find defects such as unreachable code before any test is executed.

d: A type of static testing in which people examine a work product to find anomalies, evaluate it or improve it.
tip: Review process: planning, review initiation, individual review, communication and analysis, fixing and reporting.

d: Any condition that deviates from expectations based on requirements, specifications or experience. An anomaly may or may not turn out to be a defect.
tip: Reviews and test execution report anomalies, which are then analysed.

d: A review that follows no defined process and needs no formal documented output. Its main objective is detecting anomalies.
tip: Pair review and buddy check are typical informal reviews.

d: A review led by the author, with objectives such as evaluating quality, educating reviewers, building confidence and reaching consensus.
tip: Author leads = walkthrough.

d: A review performed by technically qualified reviewers and led by a moderator, aiming to reach consensus and make decisions about a technical problem.
tip: Technical review = technical experts making decisions.

d: The most formal review type, following the complete generic process, with defined roles, entry and exit criteria and metrics. Its main goal is finding as many anomalies as possible.
tip: In an inspection the author cannot act as review leader or scribe. Metrics are collected to improve the process.

d: The person who takes overall responsibility for a review, deciding who is involved and organising when and where it takes place.
tip: Review roles: manager, author, moderator (facilitator), scribe (recorder), reviewer and review leader.

d: The review role that collects anomalies from reviewers and records review information such as decisions and new anomalies found during the meeting. Also called recorder.
tip: The moderator runs the meeting; the scribe records it.

d: A procedure used to define test conditions, design test cases and specify test data. CTFL groups techniques into black-box, white-box and experience-based.
tip: Techniques help find defects efficiently with a manageable number of tests.

d: A test technique based on the specified behaviour of the test object, independent of its implementation. CTFL covers equivalence partitioning, boundary value analysis, decision table testing and state transition testing.
tip: If the implementation changes but behaviour stays the same, black-box test cases stay valid.

d: A black-box technique that divides data into partitions expected to be processed the same way, then tests at least one value from each partition. Abbreviated EP.
tip: Each Choice coverage: every partition is covered at least once. Invalid partitions should be tested one at a time.

d: A black-box technique that tests the values at the edges of ordered equivalence partitions. In 2-value BVA each boundary and its closest neighbour are tested; in 3-value BVA both neighbours are tested too. Abbreviated BVA.
tip: Count carefully: for a range 1–100 with 2-value BVA the coverage items are 0, 1, 100 and 101.

d: A black-box technique that tests combinations of conditions and their resulting actions. Each column of the table is a rule, i.e. a combination of conditions.
tip: The usual coverage is every feasible column (rule). Full tables have 2ⁿ columns for n Boolean conditions, before infeasible ones are removed.

d: A black-box technique that models the system's states and the events that cause transitions between them, often as a state diagram or state table.
tip: Coverage criteria: all states, valid transitions (0-switch) and all transitions, including invalid ones.

d: A test technique based on the internal structure of the test object. CTFL covers statement testing and branch testing.
tip: White-box techniques cannot find missing requirements, because there is no code for them.

d: The percentage of executable statements exercised by a test suite.
tip: 100% statement coverage does not guarantee 100% branch coverage.

d: The percentage of branches, both conditional and unconditional, exercised by a test suite.
tip: 100% branch coverage implies 100% statement coverage, but not the other way round.

d: An attribute or combination of attributes derived from test conditions and used to measure coverage, for example a partition, a boundary value, a decision table column or a branch.
tip: Coverage = coverage items exercised ÷ total coverage items × 100%.

d: A test technique based on the tester's knowledge, experience and intuition. CTFL covers error guessing, exploratory testing and checklist-based testing.
tip: These techniques find defects the formal techniques may miss, but coverage is hard to measure.

d: An experience-based technique that anticipates likely errors, defects and failures from the tester's knowledge, for example by building a list of possible faults (fault attacks).
tip: Based on how the application worked before, typical developer mistakes and failures in similar applications.

d: An approach in which tests are designed, executed and evaluated at the same time while the tester learns about the test object. It is often session-based and guided by a test charter.
tip: Most useful when specifications are poor or time is short.

d: Documentation of the goal and focus of an exploratory test session.
tip: Session-based exploratory testing uses a time box and a test charter, followed by a debriefing.

d: An experience-based technique where the tester uses a list of items, notes or rules to check, based on experience of what is important or what typically fails.
tip: Checklist items should be phrased as questions and not be things that tools can check automatically.

d: Approaches that focus on avoiding defects through collaboration and communication, such as writing user stories together, defining acceptance criteria and ATDD.
tip: The goal is defect prevention, not only detection.

d: A short description of a feature from the user's perspective. It has three aspects: Card, Conversation and Confirmation (the 3 Cs).
tip: Good user stories follow INVEST: Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small and Testable.

d: The conditions a user story must meet to be accepted by stakeholders. Common formats are scenario-oriented (Given/When/Then) and rule-oriented (a bullet list or table).
tip: Acceptance criteria define the scope of the story and are the basis for acceptance tests.

d: A document that describes the objectives, resources and processes for testing, such as context, assumptions, stakeholders, scope, risks, approach, budget and schedule.
tip: Writing a test plan forces testers to think about future challenges, risks and schedules.

d: How testing will be done: the test levels, test types, test techniques, deliverables, entry and exit criteria and the degree of independence.
tip: The test approach is part of the test plan.

d: In iterative development, planning ahead for a release by defining and refining the product backlog. Testers help write testable user stories and analyse risks.
tip: Iteration planning looks ahead to the end of a single iteration; release planning looks ahead to the release.

d: Planning the work for one iteration from the iteration backlog. Testers take part in detailed risk analysis of user stories and estimate test effort.
tip: Testers help break user stories into tasks, especially testing tasks.

d: Preconditions for starting an activity, such as availability of resources, testware and an initial quality level of the test object.
tip: In agile, the Definition of Ready plays the role of entry criteria.

d: Conditions that must be met to declare an activity finished, such as achieved coverage, number of unresolved defects or completed planned tests.
tip: In agile, the Definition of Done plays the role of exit criteria. Running out of time or budget can also be a valid reason to stop.

d: Predicting the effort needed for testing. CTFL techniques: estimation based on ratios, extrapolation, Wideband Delphi and three-point estimation.
tip: Three-point: E = (a + 4m + b) ÷ 6, standard deviation SD = (b − a) ÷ 6.

d: Ordering test cases for execution. CTFL strategies are risk-based, coverage-based and requirements-based prioritisation.
tip: Dependencies between test cases may force a different order from pure priority.

d: A model showing that different test layers have different granularity: many small, fast, isolated tests at the bottom (for example unit tests) and fewer large, slow end-to-end tests at the top.
tip: The higher the layer, the less isolated and the slower the tests.

d: A model that groups test types along two axes: business-facing versus technology-facing, and supporting the team versus critiquing the product.
tip: Q1: component tests; Q2: functional and user story tests; Q3: exploratory and usability tests; Q4: non-functional tests such as performance and security.

d: A potential event, hazard, threat or situation whose occurrence causes an adverse effect. Risk level = likelihood × impact.
tip: Two attributes define a risk: likelihood and impact.

d: The measure of a risk, defined by its likelihood and impact.
tip: Higher risk level = test earlier and more thoroughly.

d: A risk related to the quality characteristics of the product, for example missing functionality, wrong calculations, poor performance or security vulnerabilities.
tip: Product risk is about the software itself; project risk is about managing the project.

d: A risk related to the management and control of the project, for example delays, staff shortages, inaccurate estimates or supplier problems.
tip: Project risks affect schedule, budget or scope.

d: Identifying risks and assessing their likelihood and impact. It is part of risk management together with risk control.
tip: Risk analysis = risk identification + risk assessment.

d: Measures taken in response to analysed risks: risk mitigation and risk monitoring.
tip: Responses to risk: mitigation by testing, acceptance, transfer or a contingency plan.

d: Testing in which activities are selected, prioritised and managed based on risk analysis and risk control.
tip: Risk affects scope, test techniques, test levels and types, effort and the priority of tests.

d: Measurements collected to show progress against the plan, for example project progress, test progress, product quality, defects, risks, coverage and cost.
tip: Metrics support test monitoring and test control.

d: A regular report during testing showing progress against the plan, impediments, metrics, new risks and work planned for the next period.
tip: Progress reports happen during testing; the completion report happens at the end.

d: A report at the end of a test activity or project summarising testing, product quality, deviations from the plan, unmitigated risks, open defects and lessons learned.
tip: It is prepared during test completion.

d: Identifying, controlling and tracking work products such as test plans, test cases and test objects, so that they are uniquely identified and version controlled.
tip: Configuration management makes sure all items are traceable to each other throughout the project.

d: The process of recognising, recording, classifying, investigating, resolving and closing defects.
tip: Defect management also handles false positives and change requests.

d: Documentation of a defect, including a unique identifier, title, date, author, test object, environment, context, description with steps to reproduce, expected and actual results, severity, priority and status.
tip: Severity = impact on the system; priority = urgency of the fix. A typo on the home page can be low severity but high priority.

d: The degree of impact a defect has on the development or operation of a component or system.
tip: Severity is usually set by testers from a technical view.

d: The level of business importance assigned to an item, for example how urgently a defect should be fixed.
tip: Priority is often set by the business or product owner.

d: Using software to perform or support test activities, such as test execution, test data generation or comparing results.
tip: Benefits: time saved, consistency, faster feedback. Risks: unrealistic expectations, underestimated effort and over-reliance on the tool.

d: Software that supports testing, for example management tools, static testing tools, test design and implementation tools, execution and coverage tools, non-functional testing tools, DevOps tools and collaboration tools.
tip: A tool only helps if it fits the process; introducing one needs planning and a pilot project.
